files.t: Properties of Shannon q-ary entropy and binary entropy functions
files.s: The binary entropy function `binEntropy p := - p * log p - (1 - p) * log (1 - p)` is the Shannon entropy of a Bernoulli random variable with success probability `p`.

h.d: They are continuous everywhere (`binEntropy_continuous` and `qaryEntropy_continuous`).
They are differentiable everywhere except at points `0` or `1` (`hasDerivAt_binEntropy` and `hasDerivAt_qaryEntropy`).

they are strictly increasing on `Icc 0 (1 - 1/q)` (`qaryEntropy_strictMonoOn`, `binEntropy_strictMonoOn`) and strictly decreasing on `Icc (1 - 1/q) 1` (`binEntropy_strictAntiOn` and `qaryEntropy_strictAntiOn`).
they are strictly concave on `Icc 0 1` (`strictConcaveOn_qaryEntropy` and `strictConcave_binEntropy`).
Binary entropy is strictly decreasing in interval [1/2, 1].
Binary entropy is strictly increasing in interval [0, 1/2].

files.s: This file proves Kraft's inequality for prefix-free codes over finite alphabets. The finite result is an immediate consequence of the Kraft–McMillan inequality; the result for arbitrary sets of codewords follows by bounding every finite partial sum.

h.d: the Kraft sum of a finite prefix-free code is at most one.
the Kraft sum of an arbitrary prefix-free code is summable.
the Kraft sum of an arbitrary prefix-free code is at most one.

files.s: This file proves the Kraft-McMillan inequality for uniquely decodable codes.

h.d: Concatenation of `r` codewords into a single string.

For a uniquely decodable code `S` over an alphabet of size `D`, `∑_{w ∈ S} D^{-|w|} ≤ 1`. The proof uses a counting argument: the `r`-th power of the Kraft sum counts concatenations of `r` codewords, weighted by length.

Auxiliary bound for Kraft–McMillan. If `S` is a finite uniquely decodable code and `1 ≤ r`, then the `r`-th power of its Kraft sum is bounded by `r * sup length`: `(∑ w ∈ S, (1 / D) ^ w.length) ^ r ≤ r * (S.sup…
Length of a concatenation of `r` codewords lies in `[r, r*sup length]` assuming `[] ∉ S`.
For uniquely decodable codes, the concatenation map is injective. This is the key property: distinct tuples of codewords produce distinct concatenations.

files.s: This file defines prefix-free codes and proves that every prefix-free code not containing the empty word is uniquely decodable.

h.d: a set of words is prefix-free if two words in the set cannot be distinct when one is a prefix of the other.
a prefix-free code not containing the empty word is uniquely decodable.
A nontrivial prefix-free code is uniquely decodable.
Any subset of a prefix-free set is prefix-free.
A prefix-free set containing the empty word is the singleton containing the empty word.

files.s: This file defines uniquely decodable codes and proves basic properties.

h.d: A set of codewords is uniquely decodable if distinct concatenations of codewords yield distinct strings.
Uniquely decodable codes cannot contain the empty string.
The flatten function is injective on lists of codewords from a uniquely decodable code.

files.s: The Hamming metric counts the number of places two members of a (finite) Pi type differ. The Hamming norm is the same as the Hamming metric over additive groups, and counts the number of places a member of a (finite) Pi type differs from zero.

h.d: the Hamming distance between `x` and `y`, the number of entries which differ.
the Hamming norm of `x`, the number of non-zero entries.

files.s: The Kullback-Leibler divergence is a measure of the difference between two measures.

h.d: Kullback-Leibler divergence between two measures, with value in `ℝ≥0∞`, defined as `∞` if `μ` is not absolutely continuous with respect to `ν` or if the log-likelihood ratio `llr μ ν` is not integrable with respect to…
the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two finite measures is zero if and only if the two measures are equal.
If `μ ≪ ν` and `μ univ = ν univ`, then `toReal` of the Kullback-Leibler divergence is equal to an integral, without any integrability condition.

**Gibbs' inequality**: the Kullback-Leibler divergence is nonnegative. Note that since `klDiv` takes value in `ℝ≥0∞` (defined when it is finite as `ENNReal.ofReal (...)`), it is nonnegative by definition.

files.t: Chain rule for the Kullback-Leibler divergence
files.s: Suppose that we have two finite joint measures on a product `𝓧 × 𝓨`, which can be decomposed as `μ ⊗ₘ κ` and `ν ⊗ₘ η`, where `μ` and `ν` are measures on `𝓧` and `κ` and `η` are Markov kernels from `𝓧` to `𝓨`.

h.d: `klDiv (μ ⊗ₘ κ) (ν ⊗ₘ η) = klDiv μ ν + klDiv (μ ⊗ₘ κ) (μ ⊗ₘ η)`
`klDiv (μ ⊗ₘ κ) (ν ⊗ₘ κ) = klDiv μ ν`
Chain rule for the integral of the log-likelihood ratio, under absolute continuity and integrability assumptions.
If the log-likelihood ration between two composition-products is integrable, then so is the log-likelihood ratio between the two measures on the first space.

files.t: Data processing inequality for the Kullback-Leibler divergence
files.s: The data processing inequality is a way to express the intuition that applying a (possibly random) transformation to random variables cannot increase the information they contain.

h.d: `klDiv (μ.map g) (ν.map g) ≤ klDiv μ ν` for a measurable function `g`.
`klDiv (μ.trim hm) (ν.trim hm) ≤ klDiv μ ν` for a sub-sigma-algebra `m` of `m𝓧` (with `hm : m ≤ m𝓧`).
`klDiv (κ ∘ₘ μ) (κ ∘ₘ ν) ≤ klDiv μ ν` for a Markov kernel `κ`.

files.t: The real function `fun x ↦ x * log x + 1 - x`
files.s: We define `klFun x = x * log x + 1 - x`. That function is notable because the Kullback-Leibler divergence is an f-divergence for `klFun`. That is, the Kullback-Leibler divergence is an integral of `klFun` composed with a Radon-Nikodym derivative.

h.d: the function `fun x : ℝ ↦ x * log x + 1 - x`. This is a continuous nonnegative, strictly convex function on $[0,∞)$, with minimum value 0 at 1.
For two finite measures `μ ≪ ν`, the function `x ↦ klFun (μ.rnDeriv ν x).toReal` is integrable with respect to `ν` iff the log-likelihood ratio `llr μ ν` is integrable with respect to `μ`.
For two finite measures `μ ≪ ν` such that `llr μ ν` is integrable with respect to `μ`, `∫ x, klFun (μ.rnDeriv ν x).toReal ∂ν = ∫ x, llr μ ν x ∂μ + ν.real univ - μ.real univ`.
The function `klFun` is nonnegative on `[0,∞)`.
The left derivative of `klFun` is `log x`. This also holds at `x = 0` although `klFun` is not differentiable there since the default value of `derivWithin` in that case is 0.
The right derivative of `klFun` is `log x`. This also holds at `x = 0` although `klFun` is not differentiable there since the default value of `derivWithin` in that case is 0.
